title: Pride And Prejudice: Chapter XXI
enhanced_title: Chapter XXI: The Departure from Netherfield and Misplaced Confidence
author: Jane Austen
description: Elizabeth comforts Jane after receiving Caroline Bingley's letter announcing the Netherfield party's sudden departure to London, revealing the manipulative schemes to separate Jane from Mr. Bingley while Elizabeth maintains her confidence in Bingley's affections and distrust of Miss Bingley's motives.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The chapter opens with Mr. Collins's reaction to Elizabeth's refusal, demonstrating Austen's skill at portraying wounded male pride through 'stiffness of manner and resentful silence' rather than explicit emotional displays. This economical characterization reveals how Collins's self-importance cannot accommodate rejection. His transferred attentions to Miss Lucas further underscore his fundamental indifference to Elizabeth as an individual, exposing the mercenary nature of his courtship.

Mr. Wickham's explanation for avoiding the Netherfield ball introduces the ongoing tension between him and Darcy, while Elizabeth's 'high approbation' of his forbearance reinforces her prejudice against Darcy and her favorable bias toward Wickham. His voluntary confession that the absence was self-imposed is carefully calculated to appear noble and self-sacrificing, further cementing Elizabeth's admiration. The walk back to Longbourn, during which he 'particularly attended to her,' deepens her partiality and sets the stage for her later misjudgment of his character.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Caroline Bingley's letter exemplifies the art of manipulative correspondence—her 'high-flown expressions' and calculated sentiments serve as both farewell and strategic warning, demonstrating how Austen uses letters as plot devices that drive emotional revelation. The letter's dual purpose is masterfully constructed: it performs affection for Jane while simultaneously planting seeds of doubt about Bingley's intentions. Elizabeth's immediate recognition of the letter's insincerity, hearing its phrases 'with all the insensibility of distrust,' marks the sharpest contrast between her own perspicacity and Jane's trusting nature.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's interpretation of Miss Bingley's letter reveals her perspicacity and protective nature toward Jane. Her immediate recognition of Caroline's schemes contrasts sharply with Jane's charitable but naive reading, highlighting the sisters' different approaches to character judgment. This divergence in perception is one of Austen's central dramatic engines: Elizabeth's clarity of sight is both her greatest strength and, in the case of Darcy and Wickham, her greatest liability.

Jane's refusal to believe ill of Caroline Bingley—insisting she is 'incapable of wilfully deceiving anyone'—represents Austen's exploration of excessive goodness as a vulnerability. Jane's charitable nature, while admirable, renders her susceptible to manipulation by those who understand that her trust will not be easily withdrawn. Elizabeth's gentle but firm counter-argument, urging Jane to 'believe her to be deceived, by all means,' is a pragmatic compromise that respects Jane's moral sensibility while still protecting her from the worst consequences of misplaced faith.

The debate between Elizabeth and Jane about Bingley's independence versus his susceptibility to influence foreshadows later revelations about Darcy's intervention. Elizabeth's confidence that those wishes, 'however openly or artfully spoken, could influence a young man so totally independent of everyone' proves ironically mistaken, as Darcy's interference will later demonstrate. This dramatic irony is one of Austen's most carefully laid traps: Elizabeth's very sharpness of judgment blinds her to the social forces that can bend even a well-meaning man's will.

The chapter concludes with Mrs. Bennet's characteristic self-absorption—her concern centers on dinner arrangements rather than Jane's heartbreak, as she resolves that 'though he had been invited only to a family dinner, she would take care to have two full courses.' This comic ending underscores the gap between maternal vanity and genuine familial support, while Elizabeth's successful comfort of Jane demonstrates her role as the family's emotional anchor. The bathos of Mrs. Bennet's consolation also serves a structural purpose, releasing the emotional tension of the sisters' private conversation and returning the narrative to the comic register that defines Austen's domestic world.

summary: Chapter XXI of Pride and Prejudice marks a pivotal turning point in Jane Bennet's romantic prospects. Following Elizabeth's rejection of Mr. Collins, the chapter focuses on Caroline Bingley's manipulative letter announcing the Netherfield party's sudden departure to London. While Jane interprets the letter's implications with charitable naivety, Elizabeth immediately recognizes Caroline's scheme to separate Jane from Mr. Bingley by encouraging a match with Miss Darcy. Elizabeth's passionate defense of Bingley's affections and her critique of Caroline's motives demonstrate her perspicacity and loyalty to her sister, though her insistence on Bingley's independence from his sisters' influence proves ironically misplaced. The chapter highlights the contrast between Elizabeth's sharp perception of others' faults and her blind spots, while Jane's excessive goodness renders her vulnerable to manipulation. The narrative concludes with Mrs. Bennet's characteristic focus on dinner arrangements rather than her daughter's emotional welfare, providing comic relief while underscoring Elizabeth's role as the family's true emotional support.
